title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_245
text: A clinical meeting of the Willesden Division was held on February 20th at the Willesden General Hospital, at which an interesting paper on manipulations for some joint conditions was read by Mr. W. M. Dickson. He said that the careful selection of cases for this form of treatment was all important. There were two main groups of painful stiff joints where, provided no infection were present, treatment by manipulation was indicated: first, following trauma, and secondly, due to postural or static defect. The majority of cases fell in the first group. The principal clinical sign was a limitation, generally more marked in one direction, of the normal range of movement. The x ray film was usually negative. The outstanding pathological lesion present was the formation of more or less dense fibrous adhesions between the joint surfaces or in the tendon sheaths. Manipulation should be undertaken when radiant heat, massage, and active and passive movements had failed. Anaesthesia was necessary as a rule. The amount of force applied should be reasonable, and in this the manipulator was guided by experience. The object aimed at was full normal range of movement in the joint. After treatment was most important. The full range of movement could only be retained by making the patient undertake full active movement of the joint as soon as he recovered from the anaesthetic, and by practising these full movements at frequent intervals. Most of these joints would not come to require manipulation were they adequately treated at the time of the receipt of the original trauma. Early voluntary movement, properly supervised, was the preventive treatment for these traumatic joint conditions.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_248
text: An interesting discussion followed the paper. On the motion of Dr. C. F. T. Scott, seconded by Dr. Charles Autty, a hearty vote of thanks was unanimously accorded to Mr. Dickson for his very practical and informative paper.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_254
text: A meeting of the Kesteven Division was held at the George Hotel, Grantham, on February 22nd, when fourteen members were present. Tea was provided by the chairman at 4 p.m. Dr. C. Frer was re elected as representative, and the new chairman was nominated.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_257
text: A most useful and instructive lecture was given by Mr. F. A. Willams Nome Nome on everyone in general practice. No greater compliment could have been paid to the lecturer than the request that copies of his address should be typed for distribution among the members present.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_260
text: Previous to the lecture reference was made by the Chairman to the King's illness. A proposition by the Secretary to hold a dance in aid of the P.M.A. Charities Fund was referred to a subcommittee.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_269
text: Sir, A leading article in the Times, and Dr. Fremantle in a letter in the Times of March 5th, express a fear that the extinction of the part time medical officer of health will widen the gap between the curative and preventive branches of medicine. As a general practitioner, with a jealous eye I have watched for many years the growth of the public medical service, but in this case I do not share that fear. I doubt whether this much desired co operation is brought about by one in twenty of the medical men in general practice doing part of the work of the public health service work which is not intimately connected with general medical practice, such as the inspection of houses, sewage systems, abattoirs, etc.; but I believe that it will be brought about by the family doctor undertaking work that his special experience and opportunities render him peculiarly fitted for, such as attendance at the ante natal, child welfare, and school clinics set up by the Ministry of Health. If they do this in collaboration with the medical officers they will appreciate still more the value and the need of the work that is being done by the public health service, and the public health service will appreciate the value of the general practitioner's special knowledge and skill.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_272
text: The work of the part time medical officer of health has been done remarkably well, often under great difficulties, but every day more is being required of him: he needs now to be a specialist with special training; he often has to act as consultant with the family doctor; and this his independent position makes it easier for him to do. If he is to excel his work must not be confined to too small an area, and in his work he must be quite independent of all inhibiting local influences and prejudices.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_275
text: The mutual recognition of the essential interdependence of the two services is growing rapidly, chiefly through the influence of the British Medical Association and Sir George Newman, the Chief Medical Officer of the Ministry of Health, who never misses an opportunity of expressing his appreciation of the value and of the need of the family doctor in the national medical service. I am, etc.,

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_278
text: Bradford on Avon, March 8th. C. E. S. FLEMMING.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_284
text: Sir, In a letter published in the Times of March 5th Dr. F. E. Fremantle, M.P., urged Parliament to reconsider the decision of the Ministry of Health that general practitioners are in future to be debarred from public health appointments; this letter was strongly supported by the Times in a leading article.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_287
text: Dr. Fremantle assumed that the British Medical Association would oppose the Government policy, on the ground that the Association feared the encroachment of the State on private practice, but the Medical Secretary of the B.M.A. (in the Times of March 6th) replied that, on the contrary, the B.M.A. supported the Government. But whether the general body of practitioners support the B.M.A. in this policy is, of course, a different matter.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_290
text: Between the Government on one hand, and Dr. Fremantle and the Times on the other, the B.M.A. is obviously in a position from which its influence, in whichever direction it is exercised, will probably have very far reaching results. Before this question is finally decided one would like to feel sure that the statement of policy quoted by Dr. Cox does represent the considered opinions of the members of the Association. This policy was adopted in 1911, and since those days there have been great changes in the conditions of general practice.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_293
text: Perhaps you will allow me to submit, very shortly, four reasons why the decision to abolish part time public health work should be reconsidered.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_296
text: 1. The State has encroached on private practice to the extent of causing very great financial anxiety.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_299
text: 2. The public object very strongly to this transference of work from the family doctor to the public health officer.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_302
text: 3. Much of the work done by public health officials could be done just as well by general practitioners.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_305
text: 4. Much of this work could be done better by general practitioners, and, what is more important, they could do public health research work that no one else can do, for the simple reason that no one else has the family doctor's knowledge of the home life of the people:

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_317
text: \\*\\* The B.M.A. policy is not that "general practitioners are in future to be debarred from public health appointments," but merely that it is desirable that the appointment of chief administrative medical officer of health should be a full time one. The B.M.A. policy, indeed, desires the encouragement of the use of private practitioners in the work of assistant medical officers. This policy has been repeatedly endorsed by the Representative Body since 1911.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_323
text: Sir, Never since I was, as a clinical clerk, warded in 1882 for a mysterious catarrhal fever not yet diagnosed, have I encountered such a terrible number of cases of intractable cough as in the present influenza epidemic; yet, as a rural practitioner, forced by circumstances to do most of my own dispensing, I find myself in a strange predicament. Hitherto it has been my practice in such cases, if adults, to add to any appropriate influenza mixture a suitable dose of heroin in some convenient form.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_326
text: Now, under the new Dangerous Drugs Acts Regulations, I am allowed to add to the ordinary tablespoonful dose lig. morph. acet. up to no less than one drachm, lig. morph. hyd. up to 52 minims, tr. opii up to 44 minims, and codeina or dionin up to any quantity, even in addition to any of the foregoing, but if I add to the whole bottle, which contains no other sedative, a minute fraction of a grain of heroin, a drug generally allowed to be not only the most suitable for the particular purpose, but far less likely than morphine or opium to induce habit, I find myself so hedged with restrictions as to prohibit entirely the dispensing of the remedy in these times of heavy pressure of work when it is most required.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_329
text: I have made efforts to discover what steps were taken by our Association to prevent this outrage, but all that I can elicit is that there was an attempt to secure, what has never been allowed in the case of morphine, and was therefore quite unlikely to be granted in the case of heroin, the exclusion from the Dangerous Drugs Acts restrictions of some proprietary or selected preparations containing heroin. Naturally this failed, and I cannot find that any further effort was made. The obvious, logical, and comparatively harmless expedient which would have completely provided all necessary safeguards, without imposing any really onerous duties—namely, to treat heroin on the lines authorized for morphine—seems never to have been put forward, or at any rate seriously pressed. Yet this expedient was so plain and natural that I had been assured monthly before by our regional medical officer that it would certainly be put into practice. Worse still, although the matter has been in debate for over seven months, and I have searched with care, I have been unable to find, during the whole year 1928, among references to dangerous drugs in the British Medical Journal, anything which conveyed even a hint that heroin was to be treated in this absurd and invidious way. Therefore no one else had a chance to supplement or support the abortive efforts of the Association.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_332
text: I feel sure that, had the matter been properly ventilated, as it should have been, the result would have been very different. A little rousing of medical and lay opinion, with perhaps a question in Parliament, or a few deputations to candidates thereto when a general election approaches, would surely have corrected one of the most illogical, ridiculous, and, from every possible point of view, indefensible pieces of mischievous grandmotherly legislation ever foisted upon a long suffering profession.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_335
text: It has never been maintained, so far as I can discover, at any conference in connexion with dangerous drugs, that the present regulations as regards morphine are considered insufficient to bring about their purpose—namely, to prevent the reimportation, in form convenient for the smuggler, of the alkaloids of opium, into countries where efforts are being made to limit the output of the raw drug, to control the stocks of morphine held by those who dispense it, and to prevent its dispensing in concentration likely to produce habit. At any rate no change has been suggested in these rules. Why it should be supposed that the same regulation would fail, in the case of heroin, to achieve the result desired, has never been explained; nor has it been revealed in what way such moderate restriction would contravene any international agreement.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_338
text: I suggest that, as this is a matter which most particularly and urgently affects rural practitioners, who must dispense, it be referred to that body, which never appears now to meet, but which achieved much useful work under its late chairman, the Rural Practitioners Subcommittee of the Insurance Acts Committee; so that steps may be taken, before the parliamentary election, to introduce a little common sense into this latest effort of the Home Office.—I am, etc.,

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_350
text: Sir, The Chartered Society of Massage and Medical Gymnastics was founded in 1894, and was incorporated by Royal Charter in 1920. Numerous well known and distinguished medical men are members of its council. I venture to think that the British Medical Association is not showing its usual wisdom when it seeks another basis of qualification or training.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_353
text: From my personal experience in private practice, in my capacity as one of the honorary medical officers of the School of Massage at the Royal Victoria Infirmary, Newcastle on Tyne, and from my knowledge of other schools at recognized medical centres, I may state that these people have a very good general education and a sound professional training. The work at the naval hospitals is carried out by chartered masseuses and sick hert stewards who have passed the society's examination.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_356
text: Unfortunately many medical men still, from ignorance or supposed cheapness, associate themselves with unqualified persons of the bonesetter variety. Our object as a profession should be to see that the general public has an efficient service in these matters. Are we attaining this object at present? I venture to say that we are not, and the fault is our own, because we countenance and employ the unqualified.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_359
text: There is, in my opinion, no need to set up a new diploma or certificate examination; we should assist the existing society by supporting parliamentary or legal action to put it on the same footing as the dental profession. By all means devise a scheme to absorb suitable lay assistants of experience, but after a given date insist on the full course and examination. If we countenance any lowering of the standard of training, or short cut to qualification, we are failing in our responsibility to the numerous students who undergo a strenuous and expensive course of education at the massage schools.—I am, etc.,

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_362
text: WHEATLEY DAVIDSON, M.D., M.R.C.P.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_371
text: A MEETING of the London Insurance Committee was held on February 28th.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_374
text: I was reported that the executive of the National Association of Insurance Committees was recommending the Minister of Health to amend the procedure in connexion with appeals to the Ministry. It is already provided that, where one of the parties to the appeal is an insurance practitioner, and the finding of the insurance committee is that the practitioner has been guilty of negligence as defined by the regulations, the person appointed to hear the appeal shall include a practitioner selected by the Minister from a panel. The National Association of Insurance Committees now asks that the tribunal shall also include a person selected by the Minister from a panel of representatives of insured persons nominated by the association.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_380
text: The Committee approved certain revisions of the model allocation and distribution schemes in order to bring them into accord with the revised regulations. These have been the subject of conference with representatives of the Panel Committee, and will now go to the Ministry for final approval. One of the points of difference between the new and the old schemes is that provision has been made in the revised scheme which releases a practitioner

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_383
text: from the obligation to provide immediate treatment for an insured person who applies to him for inclusion in his list if the name of that person is already included in the list of a practitioner practising in the same area. Another difference is that under the new scheme, in the event of a practitioner resigning during a quarter and nominating a successor to the practice, the amount of money due in respect to the practice for the quarter shall be appropriated between the two practitioners on the basis of the number of days of the quarter during which each practitioner is responsible. The previous scheme provided that the appointment to the succeeding practitioner should be in respect of those persons only who had transferred to him, the residue being payable to other practitioners accepting isolated cases.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_389
text: The chairman said that one item in the report of the Medical Service Subcommittee was a matter of congratulation to the Committee, because it meant that the Ministry had at long last seen eye to eye with them. A case came before the Committee in July, 1926, when the Committee decided that there had been failure on the part of a practitioner to comply with the terms of service. The case was subsequently remitted to the Committee by the Ministry for consideration in connexion with the withholding of a portion of the money payable to the Committee in respect of medical benefit with a view to a corresponding deduction being made from the remuneration of the practitioner. The Committee decided to adhere to its decision that in this particular case money should not be withheld. A communication had now received from the Ministry to the effect that the Minister had decided to take no further action. In two other cases reported at that meeting the Minister had withheld the sum of five pounds in each instance, and this amount was accordingly deducted from the practitioners' remuneration.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_395
text: AR a meeting of the London Panel Committee on February 26th, with Dr. H. J. CARDELL presiding, Dr. M. S. Thomson, Mr. Cecil A. Joll, and Dr. P. Hamill were appointed members of the Committee to represent the consulting staffs of medical schools.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_401
text: A report on the count of the national index register and other matters was submitted by Dr. R. A. Chase, the representative of the Committee on the Distribution Committee. He said that from the statistics of the appointed to the number of insured persons on the lists of London practitioners that going slowly down, owing principally to the movement of the insured population over the borders of the country. Thus, while London's proportion on the index register had gone down from 13.306 per cent, in 1927 to 13.277 in 1928, the proportion for Middlesex had gone up from 3.481 in 1927 to 3.576 in the succeeding year. It appeared that rather heavy reductions were made from the London figures on account of temporary residents, insured persons on the London lists who were receiving treatment somewhere else. The reductions in the case of London appeared to be twice as great as in Birmingham, for example, Dr. Chase added that the total amount for distribution for 1928 was £6,191,752 for England and Wales, or about £150,000 more than was estimated, and just over a quarter of a million remained to be distributed for that year. The excess amount over the estimate was largely due to the increase of the insured population, which had gone up by, roughly, 420,000 in 1928 as compared with 1927.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_404
text: In reply to a question as to whether any effective action could be taken by the Panel Committee with regard to the comparatively large reduction on account of temporary residents, Dr. Chase pointed out that this must be a question of the practice of London insurance practitioners in sending insured persons away for change of air.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_410
text: A deputation was appointed to discuss with representatives of the Ministry of Health the procedure in dealing with cases of alleged excesses prescribing. It was stated that the policy of the Committee up to now had been to examine each practitioner's prescribing in detail, but that, apparently, the view of the Ministry was that an easier and more practical method would be to consider the prescribing as compared with the areal average.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_416
text: In certain cases it was recommended, on consideration of the circumstances, that where a fee of one guinea for payment of an anaesthetic had been claimed, only half a guinea should be allowed, also that certain claims for payment for emergency treatment should be disallowed; in two or three instances where some question arose it was stated that the practitioners concerned were too busy attending patients to appear before the Committee, and accordingly the cases were adjourned to give the practitioners an opportunity of defending their claim in person.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_422
text: Certain proposals agreed to by representatives of the Insurance and Panel Committees were brought forward for endorsement. These related to modifications of the allocation and distribution schemes. One of the new proposals was as follows:

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_425
text: That if a practitioner who, owing to his having been granted permission to employ a permanent assistant, has been permitted to accept insured persons in excess of the maximum defined in this scheme, taken such assistant into partnership, a period of six months shall be allowed within which period the practitioners shall be required to arrange for the reduction of his personal list to a figure within the permitted maximum, that this no reduction in his remuneration shall be made during such period by reason of the fact that his list exceeds the maximum and he is not employing an assistant.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_428
text: Dr. PARTRIDGE pointed out that this provision was limited to the cases in which the assistant was taken into partnership; he thought it should be widened to cover any partner, whether previously assistant or not. An amendment to this effect was agreed to, and the clause was then approved.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_437
text: A MEETING of practitioners on the county panel was held on February 12th. The annual financial statement and report of the Panel Committee were approved. Attention was called to the surplus of income over expenditure, and to the recommendation of the Panel Committee to make a contribution to the funds of medical charities. After discussion it was decided to devote the interest on the invested funds of the Panel Committee to this purpose, the sum to be paid over to the Charities Committee of the British Medical Association. The importance of obtaining records of attendances and mileage for statistical purposes was urged upon the meeting, and several volunteers undertook the necessary work. The attention of members was called to the new regulations governing the use of dangerous drugs.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_443
text: THE Warwickshire Panel and Local Medical Committee met at Coventry on February 28th. Dr. Herbert MALLINS presiding. At the outset the chairman referred to the loss to the insurance organization in Warwickshire sustained by the death of Dr. William Cook, who for many years had represented the Panel Committee at the annual conferences of Panel Committees in London. A resolution of confidence was adopted.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_446
text: Dr. J. L. WHALLEY and the Honorary Secretary reported the steps which had been taken as the result of an interview with Dr. Anderson (Deputy Medical Secretary), as to the best method of obtaining volunteers to keep the practice statistics asked for by headquarters. As a result of the action taken the names of twenty volunteers for the rural forms, and an extra fifteen for the urban forms, had been obtained.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_449
text: It was agreed that live extract should be added to the special list provided in the distribution schemes, and that the expenditure of this should be urged on the newly appointed Advisory Committee on the Definition of Drugs for Purposes of Medical Benefit. After a discussion as to the promotion of post graduate study schemes, for which the Ministry of Health is prepared to allocate grants from the reserved portion of the Special Mileage Fund, it was decided to urge that such courses might expediently be open to suitable applicants from urban as well as from rural areas.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_452
text: Strong condemnation of the constantly increasing burdens of the Dangerous Drugs Regulations was expressed, and a resolution was adopted protesting to the Insurance Rates Committee against the further harassing requirements incorporated in the Dangerous Drugs Regulations which, in the opinion of the meeting, constitute a heavy and unjustifiable burden on practitioners.

title: BMJ_1929_03_16_vol001_nr3558_art044_pmc2450118.txt_line_455
text: After considerable discussion of the claim of a practitioner to charge his insured patient for ultra violet ray treatment, the committee resolved that, while in its opinion, treatment by ultra violet rays involved the application of special skill and experience which general practitioners as a class could reasonably be expected to possess, it was not satisfied that the doctor in question was specially qualified within the meaning of paragraph 8 (5) of Part I of the First Schedule to the Regulations.
